motive: Suspected illicit relationship with the wife
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of PW2 (wife of the deceased) and PW3 (brother of the deceased) as crucial to establish that the appellant committed the crime. The court also accepted the evidence of PWs 5 and 8 and 9 regarding the appellant's grudge against the deceased, the recovery of the axe from the scene, and the presence of human blood on the axe.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as trustworthy, noting that PW2 had no motive to implicate the appellant and that PW3's testimony was credible as he had no reason to falsely accuse the appellant.

legal_representation.state: Shishir Pinaki, Amjid Mazbool, D. Mahesh Babu

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant hacked the deceased with an axe due to a suspected illicit relationship with his wife. They presented evidence including the axe found at the scene, blood on the axe, and the testimony of PW2 and PW3, who witnessed the incident. The FIR was not considered as substantive evidence but was used to corroborate statements.
defence_argument: The defence contended that the evidence of PW2 and PW3 could not be believed as they were interested witnesses. They argued that the omission of their names in the FIR and the delay in registering the FIR cast serious doubt on the prosecution's case. They also claimed the prosecution failed to prove the motive for the murder and that the delay in reporting the incident suggested possible concoction.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the prosecution must prove the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubt. It also emphasized that motive is irrelevant when there is un-impeachable oral evidence.
precedent_relied_upon: Surjit Singh @ Gurmit Singh v. State of Punjab 1993 Supp. (1) SCC 208; Ravi Kumar v. State of Punjab (2005) 9 SCC 315; Baitullah and Another v. State of UP. (1998) 1 SCC 509; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Jeet Singh (1999) 4 SCC 370; Nathuni Yadav and Another v. State of Bihar and Another (1998) 2 SCC 238; State of West Bengal v. Oriyal Jaiswal (1994) 1 SCC 73; Jahoor and Others v. State of U.P. 1999 Supp (1) SCC 372; Tara Singh & Others v. State of Punjab 1991 Supp (1) SCC 536; Jamna v. State of U.P. 1994 Supp (1) SCC 185; Ravinder Kumar and Another v. State of Punjab (2001) 7 SCC 690
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution succeeded in establishing the guilt of the appellant beyond all reasonable doubt. The court found that the evidence of PW2 and PW3 was trustworthy and that the axe used in the crime was recovered and tested for blood.
